channel.title: The Git Reporter
channel.description: A code-native newspaper of meaningful software change.

item.title: OpenHands: separating the software agent from the sandbox it works in
item.description: A new healthy-local-backend fallback makes the project’s larger argument concrete: the thing that helps a person steer an agent must stay legible even when the agent is running somewhere else.

item.title: API Discovery: Make the Model Own Its Web Search
item.description: Mastra’s new webSearchTool is deliberately not a generic search client: it selects a provider-native tool from the active model or fails where the provider boundary is unclear.

item.title: Builder Work: A Sandbox Is Reusable Only After It Forgets
item.description: Mastra’s public sandbox-pool patch treats reuse as a recovery problem: clean the worktree, separate credentials, and assume the machine may fail before it can be claimed again.

item.title: An Agent Framework Can Carry Your Request—Not Your Responsibility
item.description: Microsoft Agent Framework's newest A2A and BYOK samples make one quiet operating rule visible: let a caller's configuration cross the boundary, but leave the host's policy and the provider's obligations where they belong.

item.title: Microsoft Agent Framework: the successor built from AutoGen and Semantic Kernel
item.description: Microsoft's new framework has migration paths for AutoGen and Semantic Kernel, but its freshest source work makes a more practical promise: carry a caller's intent across an agent boundary without letting it overrule the host that operates the run.

item.title: The Supervision Derby: four coding-agent control surfaces enter the first Diff Derby
item.description: The opening call gives Codex a narrow provisional edge for making subagent instruction precedence survive delegation and resume—but Qwen Code, Gemini CLI, and OpenHands each put a different kind of operator control on the track.

item.title: When an Agent Sees Two MCP Servers Called Docs
item.description: OpenClaw’s Code Mode has a new answer to a quietly consequential question: when several connected machines offer a server called docs , how does an agent know which one it is calling?

item.title: API Discovery: Tell an Agent When Waiting Is the Work
item.description: CrewAI’s new WaitTool gives an agent one narrow capability: let a real external job make progress before checking it again—without pretending that a pause is a status update.

item.title: PydanticAI: what type safety means when agents can act
item.description: A fresh cancellation fix draws the line clearly: typed inputs and validated outputs can discipline an agent’s interface, but a long-running run still needs a truthful answer to one operational question—did it actually stop?

item.title: Before Goose Runs a New Model, Pick Its Permission Mode
item.description: Goose has mapped Claude Opus 5 into its runtime. Before a new model reaches local tools, the operator still has to decide whether the session runs automatically, asks first, uses risk-based approval, or stays in chat.

item.title: Goose: one open agent runtime across models, tools, and local execution
item.description: A fresh Goose provider change adds Claude Opus 5 and adaptive-thinking support; the more consequential choice is still whether that model may act through local tools without asking first.

item.title: An Agent’s Answer Begins in the Harness
item.description: The model only sees the task after a runtime has edited its context, carried forward state, and decided what survived the last turn—so the first question after a bad run is what the harness made it see.

item.title: Before You Blame the Model, Inspect What the Harness Made It See
item.description: A model's next move is shaped by the tool output, trust state, history, and recovery rules a harness hands it—so a bad run is not automatically a bad model.

item.title: Cline: the supervised editor agent growing into an SDK and CLI
item.description: Cline's newest desktop work is not just another client: it moves chat toward a shared Hub that has to keep sessions, capabilities, and approvals legible across surfaces.

item.title: Mastra: turning TypeScript application primitives into agent infrastructure
item.description: Mastra's open source says the difficult part of an agent stack is not producing a turn—it is making state, resumption, tracing, and tool authority behave like application concerns.

item.title: Qwen Code: when an open model and coding agent evolve together
item.description: Qwen Code's latest trust-reload work shows what a model-aware coding agent still has to own: workspace authority, session state, tool routes, and a safe way to change the rules while work is running.

item.title: The 67,000-Star Repo That Changed What It Was
item.description: Open Interpreter’s GitHub audience remembers a Python computer agent. The code behind the same counter is now a Rust fork of Codex—and almost all of the stars arrived before that switch.

item.title: Builder Work: Search Is Another Permission Boundary
item.description: Qwen Code’s new search path treats a billed, credentialed web request as a tool that must earn its power—not as a convenience setting that quietly inherits an agent’s other privileges.

item.title: Kilo Code: from fork to agentic engineering platform
item.description: Kilo’s CLI still carries OpenCode in its source tree. Its newest code shows what a fork has to own once it starts routing work among editors, remote sessions, and a cloud service.

item.title: An Agent's Sign-In Link Is Not a Timeout
item.description: OpenWork's newest MCP work carries a provider's structured authorization link through a failed tool call, so the person who owns the account can act instead of watching an agent retry the wrong problem.

item.title: API Discovery: One Reasoning-Effort Dial Across Provider Integrations
item.description: LangChain's new reasoning_effort interface lets a builder express an effort choice once across supported chat integrations—provided the selected model profile says that choice exists.

item.title: Builder Work: Pi Counts the Work Its Agent Hides
item.description: Pi's latest accounting patch treats compaction, branch summaries, and tool-result hooks as model work with receipts—not invisible overhead beneath an agent's final answer.

item.title: The Diff Can't Be Guesswork Once an Agent Writes
item.description: OpenClaw is making a simple rule explicit: when an agent writes a file, a review surface should show the patch it can prove—and show uncertainty when it cannot.

item.title: API Discovery: Tail a Delegated Hermes Agent at Work
item.description: Hermes' public delegate_task surface can now return a live, local log for each child—useful when a background fan-out needs observation without flooding the parent conversation.

item.title: Codex Stops Asking Its Subagents the Same Question Twice
item.description: A Codex TUI patch cuts duplicate status reads by treating new, resumed, and actively streaming agent threads as different lifecycle states.

item.title: A Computer-Use Agent Needs a Second Meaning of Success
item.description: Hermes now tells a desktop-driving agent whether an input merely reached a driver or was actually confirmed to have changed the interface—and it makes foreground escalation a separate decision.

item.title: API Discovery: A Scheduler Should Ask Which France It Is In
item.description: France’s public holiday API gives an agent zone-specific statutory dates—but only a person can decide whether that means a team is unavailable.

item.title: Gemini CLI’s Caretaker Has Permission to Read, Not to Act
item.description: Gemini CLI’s new issue-triage worker gives its model a read-only repository view, then keeps labels, comments, retries, and escalation in a separate validated program.

item.title: Builder Work: When an MCP Session Dies, Rebuild the Whole Registry
item.description: Crush’s agent-attributed MCP recovery work teaches a hard-earned rule: a connection is not back until every capability it advertises is back too.

item.title: The Hard Part of an Agent Protocol Rewrite Is Yesterday
item.description: Tau is replacing its legacy agent protocol with Pi-compatible shapes, but its more consequential promise sits at the JSONL boundary: old sessions are meant to cross without pretending the old runtime still exists.
